Repeated events and a cash reserve: average cost, event probability and unfunded outcomes

Four charts show how a hypothetical annual event probability accumulates across independent years, why a reserve can cover one event but not several, and how averages differ from cash protection.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Test repeated independent events against one unreplenished reserve

Interactive planning lab

At least one modeled event within the horizon65.13%
Total modeled cost exceeds the opening reserve26.39%
Probability-weighted total event cost$5,000

Original hypothetical independent-year model, not observed household incident data or an estimate of anyone’s actual risk. Each complete year has either zero events or one event, with the same independently entered probability; years are mutually independent. Every event costs the same entered whole-CAD amount. All costs and the one opening whole-CAD reserve are in a common constant-dollar basis. The reserve is available initially, used only for these events and never replenished; there is no income, insurance reimbursement, interest, inflation, borrowing, investment or other spending. The event count follows the binomial model under these assumptions. Total cost equals count × cost per event. An unfunded cost occurs only when total cost is STRICTLY GREATER than the reserve; exactly using all of it is fully funded for this limited exercise. Probability-weighted unfunded cost sums max(total cost − reserve, 0) across all outcomes, including zero for funded outcomes. It is not a conditional tail average, a confidence limit, a worst-case amount or a recommended reserve. The count distribution retains every outcome; counts five and above share one labelled display bucket. No event timing within a year, real-world independence or statistical calibration is established.

The central idea

An average loss is a probability-weighted calculation. Test the distribution of actual possible costs against the reserve before treating that average as sufficient cash.

01

State what repeats and what stays fixed

A statement such as “a 10% chance each year” needs more detail before it can support a long-term cash calculation. It must identify the event, whether several can occur in one year, whether the chance changes and whether one year's outcome affects another.

This illustration uses an invented event with a 10% probability in each of ten complete years. Each year permits either zero events or one event, with the same probability every time. The years are assumed mutually independent.

Every event costs CAD 5,000 in a common constant-dollar basis. One CAD 5,000 reserve is available at the start and is not replenished. It earns no interest and pays no other expenses. These restrictions deliberately make the difference between frequency, severity and cash coverage visible.

NIST's binomial-distribution explanation supplies the mathematical reference for counting repeated two-outcome trials with a fixed probability. The annual probabilities here are independently authored inputs. The model does not fit a historical dataset or infer how likely a repair, job loss or health event is for a real household.

02

Calculate at least one event through the no-event outcome

Under the independence assumption, the chance of no event in one year is 90%. The chance of no event in all ten years is 0.910, approximately 34.87%. Subtracting that result from 100% gives approximately 65.13% for at least one event.

Adding 10% ten times gives an expected count of one event, rather than a 100% probability that an event occurs. Expected counts can exceed one over longer periods; probabilities remain between zero and one.

The first curve therefore answers a precise question: what is the modeled chance of one or more events within the selected number of years? It does not say exactly one event will occur, identify its date or establish the probability of a cash shortage.

The distinction matters because the reserve can fund one default event exactly. At least one event and an unfunded outcome are different sets of outcomes. The second curve applies the reserve to the entire event-count distribution.

03

Retain the chance of no event and multiple events

The expected event count is the number of years multiplied by the annual event probability: ten times 10%, or one. That average can coexist with substantial chances of zero events, one event and several events.

The distribution chart displays exact counts through four events, then combines all counts of five or more in one clearly labelled tail. No probability is discarded. The cost model continues to use every exact count through the full number of years.

The combined tail is a display bucket, not an outcome of exactly five events. Multiplying that bucket's probability by five would understate the contribution from six or more events. Grouping a visual does not justify changing the calculation beneath it.

At the defaults, the CAD 5,000 reserve covers zero or one event. Two or more cost more than the reserve, creating an approximately 26.39% modeled chance of an unfunded amount over ten years. This is smaller than the chance of any event, while still positive even though the expected count is only one.

04

An average cost is not a guaranteed cash requirement

The probability-weighted total cost is expected event count times cost per event. The default is one times CAD 5,000, or CAD 5,000. That equals the assigned reserve, but it does not mean every possible cost is funded.

A ten-year outcome with no event spends none of the reserve. One event spends it exactly. Two events cost CAD 10,000 and leave CAD 5,000 unfunded. The unused reserve in the zero-event outcome cannot be transferred across possible futures to pay the second event in another outcome.

The model calculates unfunded cost separately for each count: the greater of zero and total cost minus the reserve. It then weights those amounts by their probabilities. The default probability-weighted unfunded cost is approximately CAD 1,743.39.

Subtracting the reserve from the average total cost would instead give zero and lose the distinction between funded and unfunded states. Averaging first and applying a floor afterward is a different operation from applying the floor to each state and then averaging.

05

Separate using the reserve from needing more than the reserve

The shortfall condition is strict: cumulative modeled cost must be greater than the assigned reserve. A CAD 5,000 event against CAD 5,000 available uses all the reserve but creates no unfunded amount in this limited exercise.

That does not establish that ending with no reserve is suitable for a household. It only keeps the mathematical question consistent. If a separate minimum cash floor is required, it needs an additional definition rather than silently relabeling equality as a shortfall.

The weighted unfunded amount is an unconditional average over all outcomes, including zero in funded states. It is not the average conditional on a shortfall, a statistical confidence limit or the worst possible loss.

A zero cost per event leaves the event probabilities unchanged while making all modeled costs and funding gaps zero. A sufficiently large reserve can fund every permitted outcome without changing event frequency. Those checks help distinguish what each input actually affects.

06

Use the result as a conditional scenario, then restore real planning detail

The matrix varies annual probability and horizon while holding the loss amount and reserve fixed. It shows sensitivity to two independent assumptions. The cells do not recommend a confidence target or claim that one reserve protects a real household at the displayed percentage.

Real events can cluster, change in frequency, happen more than once a year or produce different costs. A household may also rebuild its reserve, receive insurance payments, earn interest or face unrelated expenses. Each change can alter this distribution and needs an appropriate model.

FCAC's emergency-fund guidance discusses money set aside for unexpected expenses and the importance of access. This article does not replace a full dated cash plan with its probability-weighted loss. It includes no replenishment schedule and does not locate the year of a funding gap.

Use an evidence-supported definition and probability range where available, then test the size and timing of costs against resources actually available. Keep annual incidence, cumulative event probability, the amount at risk and reserve funding separate. The four charts make those distinctions inspectable without turning a hypothetical probability into a personal forecast.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Every probability, cost and reserve is an invented assumption. The model permits at most one event per year, assumes identical independent years and holds one reserve without replenishment. It estimates no real household incident rate or recommended emergency-fund target.
